chunks.title: About Brian
chunks.text: Brian Fu is a software engineer and a Computer Science student at Texas A&M University, graduating in December 2027. Brian's legal first name is Jiacheng, but he goes by Brian. Brian is based in Austin, Texas, where he lives. Brian speaks English and Mandarin Chinese, both natively. Brian is a permanent U.S. resident with a green card (not a U.S. citizen), so he is authorized to work in the United States and does not need visa sponsorship. Brian is open to 2027 internships: he is seeking Summer 2027 software engineering and security internships. If you are looking to hire an intern for 2027, Brian is available: email him at brian.fu123321@gmail.com. Brian gravitates to problems where correctness is checkable: compilers, backends, and the security boundaries in between. Brian is currently employed part-time at ThingsX as an application security and full-stack engineer. You can contact Brian by email at brian.fu123321@gmail.com. Brian is on LinkedIn at linkedin.com/in/jiachengfu. Brian's GitHub is github.com/jiacheng-fu. Brian does not share a phone number here. Brian's resume is not posted here; his LinkedIn, linkedin.com/in/jiachengfu, covers his experience.

chunks.title: Career at a glance
chunks.text: Brian has worked at three companies: ThingsX, Mesa, and United Micro Technology. Brian's current job is at ThingsX, where he has been an Application Security Engineer and Full-Stack Engineer on a part-time contract since June 2026. From August 2026 to October 2026, Brian was also the Founding Engineer (Backend & ML) at Mesa. Brian is open to 2027 internships. Brian has done two internships, both at United Micro Technology: Software Engineering Intern from June 2024 to August 2024, and LLVM Compiler Intern from May 2025 to August 2025. Brian's projects are Axle (since January 2026), Project Horizon (since August 2023), Wild West Party Game (a HowdyHack 2024 team build), DeskStats (2026), CarStatus (2026), and this website (2026). Brian built Axle as its sole author and builds Project Horizon solo; Wild West Party Game was a team build. Brian's oldest project still in progress is Project Horizon, which he started in August 2023. Brian studies Computer Science with a Minor in Mathematics at Texas A&M University, with a 3.87/4.00 GPA, and graduates in December 2027.

chunks.title: ThingsX
chunks.text: Since June 2026, Brian has been at ThingsX as an Application Security Engineer and Full-Stack Engineer, on a part-time contract. Brian works on ThingsX's production multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform, built with TypeScript, Deno, PostgreSQL, React, and REST APIs. At ThingsX, Brian has authored and resolved roughly 40 tickets (quality-of-life improvements, defects, and security fixes), owning each change from the schema migration through the API layer to the operator-facing UI. Brian's UI work at ThingsX includes sortable data tables, chart rendering and label-overlap fixes, report filter behavior, account status displays, and role and session state. In his security work at ThingsX, Brian has remediated 50+ production vulnerabilities across access-control, injection, and race-condition classes. Brian fixed a cross-tenant authorization gap at ThingsX by moving privileged-function authorization server-side onto session auth; he proved the fix by reproducing the exploit in reverse, and regression-tested it so the entire bug class fails the build. At ThingsX, Brian built a 13-stage, one-command CI/CD pipeline enforced by a pre-push git hook: typecheck, builds, unit tests, negative Row-Level Security probes, and data-integrity invariants. Brian also eliminated a job-queue data-loss bug at ThingsX with exactly-once TOCTOU guards, verified under 20-way parallel load.

chunks.title: Mesa
chunks.text: From August 2026 to October 2026, Brian was the Founding Engineer (Backend & ML) at Mesa, an early-stage startup. As the sole owner of Mesa's backend, Brian built the production document intake pipeline end to end: quarantine, malware scanning, deduplication, parsing, OCR, segmentation, and classification. Brian covered Mesa's pipeline with roughly 1,880 tests, on a multi-tenant Postgres layer that enforces row-level security on every tenant table. Mesa's pipeline sustained about 790 pages per hour per graphics card, on a tiered text-recognition stack Brian built with Paddle OCR and ONNX Runtime, behind a Postgres work queue whose workers scale to zero when idle. Brian's document classifier at Mesa, a production machine learning system, automated 54.2% of known-source document classification at 99.1% precision in 5.5 milliseconds, rising to 88.7% at 98.9% precision with a language-model tier. For that classifier, Brian labeled a 9,100-document corpus and shipped three tiers: template matching, title rules, and a term-frequency logistic regression. Brian's pre-registered audit of ten classifier variants then established that the model's ceiling was label source diversity, not features. Brian designed Mesa's production cloud deployment to run at roughly $1,100 a month against a $2,500 budget ceiling, across a 20x range of document volume. Brian also shipped Mesa's frontend-backend contract: token-based tenant identity, read models with committed schemas and generated types, and browser-direct uploads with per-file idempotency keys.

chunks.title: United Micro · compiler intern
chunks.text: From May 2025 to August 2025, the summer of 2025, Brian was an LLVM Compiler Intern at United Micro Technology. At his compiler internship, Brian worked on United Micro Technology's LLVM compiler backend in C++, for a proprietary vector DSP: he implemented instruction selection rules, register allocation paths, and lowering strategies. Brian also assessed vector instruction extensions for NPU-integrated workloads. Brian enabled early-stage architectural modeling at United Micro Technology by translating ISA specifications into processor description files. Brian's technical report on backend design tradeoffs steered United Micro Technology's subsequent vDSP ASIP compiler work.

chunks.title: United Micro · software intern
chunks.text: From June 2024 to August 2024, the summer of 2024, Brian was a Software Engineering Intern at United Micro Technology. Brian built a Python ingestion system that normalized third-party vendor register descriptions into United Micro Technology's internal SystemRDL representation, cutting the effort to onboard externally acquired IP by an estimated 60-70%. Brian extended the open-source SystemRDL toolchain with custom Jinja2-templated exporters that emit synthesizable RTL, C headers, and documentation in the company's internal file structure. Brian's SystemRDL tool shipped to real users: it was embedded in the production chip design flow, packaged with Poetry for reproducible installs, and used daily by 200+ engineers.

chunks.title: Axle
chunks.text: Axle is an AI-powered used-car search that Brian has been building since January 2026: describe the car you want in plain English, and it finds, ranks, and compares real listings from nearby dealers. Brian built and deployed Axle as its sole author, taking it from a TAMUhack prototype (built for the Toyota track) to a deployed product with a React and Vite frontend, a FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL, and auth. Axle's LLM pipeline (OpenRouter) turns free-form text into validated, structured JSON, with schema sanitization, a 40-entry feature-alias map with fuzzy matching, and two-tier model routing with failover: a cheap model for routine parses and a capable one when the request is ambiguous. Axle ranks results with a 10-level progressive constraint-relaxation algorithm over a weighted scoring engine, so a search returns useful matches instead of an empty page when nothing satisfies every filter. Axle stays inside a 1,000-call/month API budget, the provider's free tier, through multi-tier caching across memory, disk, and AWS DynamoDB (NoSQL, with TTL expiry). Axle runs serverless on AWS Lambda and API Gateway, with its frontend on CloudFront and S3. Axle's backend is FastAPI on AWS Lambda (Python 3.12, arm64) behind API Gateway through Mangum, defined in a SAM template, with the Lambda's role scoped to its single DynamoDB table. Axle caches listings in DynamoDB because Lambda filesystems are ephemeral and per-instance, so a disk cache stops protecting the API quota once the app runs serverless. Axle is built with React, TypeScript, Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, AWS, and REST APIs. Brian used Axle himself when he bought his own car. Axle's source code is public on GitHub at github.com/jiacheng-fu/axle.

chunks.title: Project Horizon
chunks.text: Project Horizon is a narrative exploration game that Brian has been building solo in C# and Unity since August 2023. Project Horizon is written in C# on the Unity engine. Brian owns Project Horizon's full development cycle: a branching storyline system with multiple outcomes, core mechanics, state management, player progression, and UX. Project Horizon has branching dialogue with voiceover sync, third-person traversal, and a life system. Project Horizon's 2.5D art direction is inspired by the look of Octopath Traveler, which Brian has never actually tried.

chunks.title: Wild West Party Game
chunks.text: Wild West Party Game is a real-time multiplayer western party game that Brian built with a team in 24 hours at HowdyHack 2024, in September 2024. In Wild West Party Game, players join a lobby from their phones for drawing and prompt rounds, with AI-generated art. Brian's work on Wild West Party Game included its inter-scene mechanics, transitions, and UI, for a working multiplayer prototype with real-time connectivity across distinct client states. Wild West Party Game was built with Next.js, TypeScript, React, Socket.IO, Python, and OpenAI.

chunks.title: DeskStats
chunks.text: DeskStats is a native desktop widget for Apple Silicon Macs that Brian built in 2026 with Swift, SwiftUI, AppKit, and IOKit. DeskStats shows per-core CPU, GPU, memory, power draw, and charging rate, read straight from IOKit. DeskStats needs no permissions and uses about 1.4% of one CPU core. Brian decided to build DeskStats because he missed the hardware readout of Windows Task Manager and found no equivalent for his MacBook.

chunks.title: CarStatus
chunks.text: CarStatus is a command-line tool that Brian built in 2026 to fetch a car's odometer, fuel, and battery through Smartcar's v3 API. Brian built CarStatus against a BMW, pulling its odometer, fuel, battery, and GPS coordinates through the Smartcar API. CarStatus includes the webhook setup that Smartcar's documentation skips. CarStatus is written in JavaScript on Node.js. The CarStatus recording on the projects page runs the tool in a real terminal against a Smartcar Simulator car, through Smartcar's real v3 API.

chunks.title: This website
chunks.text: Brian built this website, his portfolio, in 2026 with the React framework, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js; it is his own build, not a template. The 3D keyboard on this website shows Brian's stack; the keyboard idea and keycaps are from Naresh Khatri's MIT-licensed portfolio. The photo at the top of this website was taken on the Space Needle in Seattle, not in Austin. This website's question machine works by retrieval: it searches this archive about Brian with BM25 keyword scoring (no embeddings) inside your browser, and quotes the closest-matching sentences word for word. Switched on, the machine's optional LLM, Qwen3-0.6B, runs in your browser on your own GPU. This website has no server and no API key, and nothing you type into this machine leaves your browser. A note a visitor teaches this machine stays only in that visitor's browser tab and is gone on reload.

chunks.title: Languages
chunks.text: Brian's tech stack spans programming languages, full-stack web and machine learning tools, and systems, cloud, and security work. Brian speaks two languages natively, English and Mandarin Chinese. Brian codes in C++, Java, Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, C#, SQL (PostgreSQL and PL/pgSQL), Bash, Haskell, HTML, and CSS. Brian has also written Swift, for DeskStats, and a GLSL shader for an earlier version of this website. The programming languages Brian is most comfortable in are Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and C++. In a coding interview, Brian prefers to code in Python 3.

chunks.title: Full-Stack & ML
chunks.text: On the web, Brian builds with React, Next.js, Node.js, Deno, Vite, and FastAPI, with SQLAlchemy, Alembic, and Pydantic in Python. Brian designs REST APIs and PostgreSQL schemas and migrations, and implements authentication and authorization, caching, and responsive UIs. For machine learning, Brian has used scikit-learn, OCR with PaddleOCR, ONNX Runtime with CUDA, LLM integration, and evaluation design; at Mesa, Brian put OCR and a document classifier into production. Brian builds games in Unity.

chunks.title: Systems, Cloud & Security
chunks.text: For version control and CI, Brian uses Git, GitHub, and GitHub Actions, and he has built CI/CD pipelines. Brian ships with Docker and Docker Compose, tests with pytest and unit tests, and has built job queues and TOCTOU race-condition tests. For cloud, Brian uses AWS (Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, IAM, S3, and CloudFront), and he has also used Supabase (PostgREST and Auth), MinIO, and Vercel. Brian's systems work includes LLVM compiler backends and SystemRDL/RTL code generation. Brian's security skills include multi-tenant isolation, Row-Level Security, threat modeling, OWASP vulnerability classes, and exploit-regression validation.

chunks.title: Hackathons
chunks.text: Brian has done three hackathons: HowdyHack 2024, TAMUhack 2025, and the TAMUhack where Axle began. At HowdyHack 2024, Brian and his team built Wild West Party Game in 24 hours. At TAMUhack 2025, Brian's team pivoted mid-event and rebuilt their idea on Project Horizon, Brian's own Unity game. At TAMUhack 2025, Brian built the team's Unity gameplay layer: the dialogue engine, third-person movement, the life system, NPC behavior, and scene triggers; his teammates built a React dashboard and a machine learning notebook. Axle started as Brian's TAMUhack prototype for the Toyota track.

chunks.title: Class work & open source
chunks.text: In CSCE 331, Foundations of Software Engineering, Brian's Team 14 built a point-of-sale system for Sharetea as its second project; its generated Javadoc is public on Brian's GitHub, and the rest lives in the private class repository. Brian forked PeakRDL-html, the open-source tool that generates register-map documentation from SystemRDL, the register-description format he worked with at United Micro Technology. Brian's code is on GitHub at github.com/jiacheng-fu, including his TAMUhack 2025 team project.

chunks.title: How Brian works
chunks.text: Brian's engineering philosophy: a fix you can't demonstrate failing beforehand and passing afterwards isn't a fix. The areas of software Brian is most interested in are web apps, data processing systems, and security and privacy. Brian is keen on backend, frontend, and full-stack work equally. Outside computer science, Brian's classes at Texas A&M have included Global Cinema, Climate Change, Intro to Psychology, and beginning badminton.

chunks.title: Background
chunks.text: Brian's hometown is Xi'an, China, where he was born; he later moved to Austin, Texas. Xi'an is Brian's favorite place: it holds an unshakable, golden nostalgia for him that nothing will beat. When Brian was young, he had a pet hamster. Brian got into programming because he enjoyed fixing problems; software engineering came naturally to him as technology evolved.

chunks.text: Brian's hobbies outside programming are video games and going to the gun range. Brian's fun fact: he can crack all of his fingers just by making a fist.

chunks.title: What's next
chunks.text: Brian's honest first answer to what he wants to work on after graduating is anything that pays in this market. After he graduates, the field Brian finds most interesting is robotics, AI, and autonomous decision-making with hardware. Brian's experience leans full-stack. Brian's proudest projects are Axle and then DeskStats, because both fix problems he actually had: he used Axle to buy his own car, and built DeskStats for his own MacBook.
